faq.title: Questions
faq.q1: What happens if DBackup becomes unavailable - can I still restore?
faq.a1: Yes. Every backup is a standard database dump encrypted with open AES-256-GCM. With the key from your Recovery Kit and a standalone Node.js script, you can decrypt and restore without DBackup running at all.
faq.a2: <mysql>MySQL</mysql>, <mariadb>MariaDB</mariadb>, <postgresql>PostgreSQL</postgresql>, <mongodb>MongoDB</mongodb>, SQLite, <redis>Redis</redis>, Valkey, Microsoft SQL Server, Azure SQL Database (beta), and Firebird (beta), with more engines added regularly. <all>See every integration</all>.
faq.q3: Can DBackup back up files and folders, not just databases?
faq.a3: Yes. Any storage adapter can serve as a directory source - local paths, SFTP, SMB, FTP, WebDAV, S3, Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, rsync over SSH, or Docker volumes read through the daemon. Files and databases can share one job, so the dump and the data directory that belongs to it land in the same archive and the same restore point. There is no agent to install: DBackup reads whatever those protocols reach. That agentless design is also its limit - a full run pulls the tree to the DBackup host and stages it there before packing, so it wants roughly twice the source size in free space and every byte crosses the network twice. It is built for the files that belong to the applications you already back up databases for, not for bulk media libraries; for those, restic or Borg run on the machine itself and are the better tool.
faq.q4: Can DBackup back up Docker volumes?
faq.a4: Yes, currently in beta. Pick the volumes from a list of what the Docker daemon can see, locally through its socket or on another host over SSH, and DBackup mounts them into a short-lived helper container to read them. Containers holding a selected volume are stopped for the read and started again right afterwards, per volume rather than for the whole job, and you can switch that off for data that is safe to copy live. Restoring goes back into the same volume or into a new one, though directory permissions and empty directories are not carried back yet, which is what keeps it in beta.
faq.q5: Does DBackup deduplicate like restic or Borg?
faq.a5: Not globally, and that is a deliberate trade. Incremental backups store whole changed files and reference unchanged ones in earlier archives of the same chain, so every archive stays a plain TAR you can open with tar -xf or a documented format one Node.js script reads. A chunk store would save more space but would make the backup a repository only its own tool can open - which is the lock-in DBackup exists to avoid.
faq.q6: Is there a hosted or cloud version?
faq.a6: No. DBackup is self-hosted only, distributed as a single Docker image you run on your own infrastructure.
faq.q7: What license is DBackup released under?
faq.a7: GPL-3.0. The source code is fully open and available on GitHub.
faq.q8: Can I send one backup to multiple storage destinations?
faq.a8: Yes. Multi-destination jobs upload each backup to several storage adapters at once for redundancy or off-site copies.

dbackup-agent.title: DBackup Agent
dbackup-agent.description: A small container on the target host that DBackup talks to instead of opening an SSH session, for hosts where SSH access is not an option. Dumps still stream back to DBackup for compression and encryption, so the encryption key and the storage credentials never leave it.

sync-jobs.title: Sync Jobs
sync-jobs.description: A second kind of job next to backups: keep a target in step with a source on its own schedule. Copy a file or database backup onto another host, or replicate one database into another, without building a backup and restoring it by hand every time.

stream-based-backup-pipeline.title: Stream-based Backup Pipeline
stream-based-backup-pipeline.description: Opt-in "Large DB Mode" that pipes dumps directly to storage without staging on disk first, with parallel multi-destination upload and inline checksums for databases too large for local /tmp.

runner-resilience.title: Runner Resilience
runner-resilience.description: Exponential backoff retry logic for transient errors, plus a dead letter queue for jobs that fail repeatedly and need investigation.

restic-storage-backend.title: Restic Storage Backend
restic-storage-backend.description: Restic as a storage destination with block-level deduplication and rsyncable compression, using its own repository, browsing, and retention model instead of file-based storage.

encryption-key-rotation.title: Encryption Key Rotation
encryption-key-rotation.description: Rotate the system ENCRYPTION_KEY without downtime, re-encrypting all stored secrets with the new key.

user-invite-flow.title: User Invite Flow
user-invite-flow.description: Email-based user invitations with a forced password change on first login, built on the existing SMTP notification adapter.

backup-tags-annotations.title: Backup Tags & Annotations
backup-tags-annotations.description: Manually tag backups (e.g. "pre-migration"), pin them to protect against retention deletion, and filter by tag in the Storage Explorer.

backup-anomaly-detection.title: Backup Anomaly Detection
backup-anomaly-detection.description: Alert when a backup's size deviates significantly from previous runs, plus a scheduled "test restore" task.

prometheus-metrics-endpoint.title: Prometheus Metrics Endpoint
prometheus-metrics-endpoint.description: A /metrics endpoint exposing backup count, duration, size, success rate, and queue depth, plus a ready-made Grafana dashboard.

backup-size-limits-alerts.title: Backup Size Limits & Alerts
backup-size-limits-alerts.description: Per-job configurable thresholds that warn when a backup is unexpectedly larger or smaller than expected.

backup-drift-detection.title: Backup Drift Detection
backup-drift-detection.description: Compare a database's current state against its last backup and alert when it has drifted significantly (new tables, size growth, dropped objects).

server-health-dashboard.title: Server Health Dashboard
server-health-dashboard.description: Per-adapter server health metrics (uptime, active connections, running queries, replication status) as a pre-backup health indicator.

direct-sql-execution.title: Direct SQL Execution
direct-sql-execution.description: Run custom SQL queries against configured sources from the web UI, read-only by default with write access behind a separate permission.

query-library.title: Query Library
query-library.description: Pre-built query templates for common tasks like user management and table maintenance, available as quick actions in the UI.

user-privileges-viewer.title: User & Privileges Viewer
user-privileges-viewer.description: Read-only view of database users and their permissions, to verify the backup user has sufficient privileges as a security audit helper.

storage-trend-graph.title: Storage Trend Graph
storage-trend-graph.description: Historical database size over time derived from backup metadata, with growth-rate visualization for capacity planning.

e2e-test-suite.title: End-to-End Test Suite
e2e-test-suite.description: Playwright/Cypress coverage for critical flows - login, create job, run backup, restore, verify - running in CI.

internationalization.title: Internationalization (i18n)
internationalization.description: Multi-language UI support with room for community-contributed translations.

high-contrast-mode.title: High-Contrast Mode
high-contrast-mode.description: A high-contrast theme next to light and dark, for better readability and accessibility.

oracle-support.title: Oracle Support
oracle-support.description: Oracle Database as a new supported source, using RMAN or Data Pump exports.

influxdb-support.title: InfluxDB Support
influxdb-support.description: InfluxDB as a new supported source for backing up time-series data.

redesigned-interface.title: Redesigned Interface
redesigned-interface.description: Every page is rebuilt in a new design that also works on phones and tablets, with a search across all jobs, connections, backups and runs. New pages for the backups, the databases and the history of each run, a Quick Setup that adds the first backup in one place, and notification emails in the same look.

single-database-restores-downloads.title: Single Database Restores & Downloads
single-database-restores-downloads.description: Restore or download one database out of a multi-database backup, reading only that database from the destination. Old execution logs and history entries can be cleaned up automatically, and Settings shows and optimizes the size of the DBackup database.

300-github-stars.title: 300 GitHub Stars
300-github-stars.description: DBackup crossed 300 stars on GitHub, thanks to everyone in the community.

azure-sql-database-support.title: Azure SQL Database Support
azure-sql-database-support.description: Azure SQL Database as a new source in beta, backed up through a BACPAC export, plus an hourly tier for Smart (GFS) retention policies.

docker-volume-backups.title: Docker Volume Backups
docker-volume-backups.description: Docker volumes as a backup source (beta), listed from the target host the way databases already are, so you pick them instead of typing paths. Containers using a selected volume are stopped for the export and started again afterwards, which you can turn off per source when the data is safe to copy live.

file-folder-backups.title: File & Folder Backups
file-folder-backups.description: Directory and file sources with a seekable, per-entry encrypted archive format, incremental backup chains, byte-range restores, and a completely rebuilt Recovery Kit.

200-github-stars.title: 200 GitHub Stars
200-github-stars.description: DBackup crossed 200 stars on GitHub, thanks to everyone in the community.

firebird-support.title: Firebird Support
firebird-support.description: Firebird (3.x/4.x/5.x) as a supported database source, with direct and SSH connection modes.

valkey-support.title: Valkey Database Support
valkey-support.description: Valkey as a database source, using the same RDB backup mechanism as Redis.

notification-templates.title: Notification Templates
notification-templates.description: Reusable, per-channel, event-filtered notification templates replacing flat per-job notification config.

backup-integrity-verification.title: Backup Integrity Verification
backup-integrity-verification.description: SHA-256/MD5 checksums, on-demand Verify Now, native checksum verification across adapters, and scheduled integrity checks.

vault-credential-profiles-extended.title: Vault Credential Profiles for Webhooks & OAuth
vault-credential-profiles-extended.description: Credential vault profiles extended to WEBHOOK, OAUTH, and TOKEN types.

database-explorer-version-history.title: Database Explorer Version History
database-explorer-version-history.description: An engine-version timeline and change log per database source.

database-explorer-drill-down.title: Database Explorer
database-explorer-drill-down.description: A table/data viewer with pagination, search, and schema inspection across all adapters.

templates-system.title: Templates System
templates-system.description: A dedicated Templates page with reusable Retention Policies, Naming Templates, and Schedule Presets, assignable across jobs.

credential-profile-system.title: Credential Profile System
credential-profile-system.description: Centralized, encrypted Credential Profiles that adapters reference instead of storing secrets inline, plus one-click cloning for sources, destinations, and jobs.

live-history-redesign.title: Live History Redesign
live-history-redesign.description: Pipeline-stage tracking with real-time speed and progress for every backup and restore.

ssh-remote-execution.title: SSH Remote Execution
ssh-remote-execution.description: Run backups directly on the remote database host via SSH, without a local database client.

https-by-default.title: HTTPS by Default & Certificate Management
https-by-default.description: Built-in HTTPS with auto-generated certificates by default, plus a Certificate Management UI.

first-stable-release.title: First Stable Release
first-stable-release.description: The first stable release, stabilizing the platform after the beta phase.

compression.gzipText: Works with every server. A safe choice when you do not want to think about it.
compression.lz4Text: Barely slows the dump down and leaves the file a little larger. Good for big databases and short nights.
compression.zstdText: Small files at a good speed. Levels above 19 need a lot of memory.
compression.noneText: pg_dump writes the dump uncompressed, and DBackup can compress it with Gzip or Brotli instead.

options.snapshotText: Reads InnoDB tables at one point in time without blocking writes. Off, the tables of each database are locked while it is dumped.
options.routinesText: Dumps the routines of each database with its tables.
options.eventsText: Dumps the scheduled events of each database.
options.check: Before each dump DBackup checks what the login may read. Where it may not read the events or the body of a routine, that database is dumped without them, with a warning on the run.

postgresql.description: Self-hosted PostgreSQL backups with pg_dump. Scheduled, compressed with Gzip, LZ4 or Zstd, with AES-256-GCM encryption and kept on S3, SFTP, a NAS or a cloud drive. Open source.
postgresql.lead: DBackup runs pg_dump on a schedule, encrypts the dumps with AES-256-GCM when the job has a key and keeps them on the storage you choose. Directly or over SSH, with the restore in the same app.
postgresql.fact3Label: Over SSH, pg_dump runs on your server
postgresql.fact4Label: Pick databases and give them new names
postgresql.dumpStep: pg_dump -F c writes a custom-format dump of each database, one after the other.
postgresql.compressStep: Gzip, LZ4 or Zstd inside pg_dump, at a level you pick. Or none, and DBackup can compress the dump instead.
postgresql.featureText: The job decides how pg_dump compresses, with a level between faster and smaller. While it does, DBackup leaves the dump as it is, so nothing is compressed twice.
postgresql.featureNote: The job form reads the version of your server and offers LZ4 from PostgreSQL 14 and Zstd from 16.
postgresql.archiveText: Pick some databases of a server, or all of them. Each gets its own dump, and all of them land in one TAR with a manifest and an index of their checksums.
postgresql.archive1: Leave the pick empty and every run finds the databases again, new ones included.
postgresql.archive2: Restore one database and leave the others alone, under its own name or a new one.
postgresql.archive3: Unencrypted, the archive opens with tar -xf, and the dumps inside are plain pg_dump files.
postgresql.restoreLead: Every dump is what pg_dump wrote. Keep the Recovery Kit somewhere DBackup cannot reach, and any machine with Node.js and pg_restore 18 brings the data back.
postgresql.userText: Reading is enough for the backup. When a restore needs more, the app asks for an admin login once.
postgresql.q1: Which PostgreSQL versions does DBackup support?
postgresql.a1: PostgreSQL 12 to 18. The image ships pg_dump from PostgreSQL 18, which reads every older server in that range. Over SSH, the pg_dump on your server does the work.
postgresql.q2: Does the backup include roles and tablespaces?
postgresql.a2: No. DBackup runs pg_dump for each database and never pg_dumpall, so roles and tablespaces are not in the backup. A restore leaves out owners and grants, so the restored objects belong to the login that restores them.
postgresql.q3: Can DBackup back up a server it cannot reach directly?
postgresql.a3: Yes, over SSH, which is in beta. DBackup logs into the server, runs pg_dump there and streams the dump back. pg_dump, pg_restore and psql have to be installed on that server.
postgresql.q4: Does the backup user need to be a superuser?
postgresql.a4: No. Reading the data is enough. From PostgreSQL 14 the pg_read_all_data role covers every database, on older servers you grant CONNECT and SELECT per database.
postgresql.q5: Can I restore a backup without DBackup?
postgresql.a5: Yes. The Recovery Kit gets the dumps out, encrypted or not, with nothing but Node.js. pg_restore reads them back, version 18 for dumps from the Docker image, since pg_restore never reads a dump from a newer pg_dump.

mysql.description: Self-hosted MySQL backups for MySQL 5.7 to 9. Dumps from one consistent snapshot with routines and events by default, with AES-256-GCM encryption, kept on S3, SFTP, a NAS or a cloud drive. Open source.
mysql.lead: DBackup dumps every database from one consistent snapshot, with its routines and events unless you turn them off. It encrypts the dumps with AES-256-GCM when the job has a key and keeps them on the storage you choose.
mysql.fact3Label: Over SSH, the dump runs on your server
mysql.fact4Label: Pick databases and give them new names
mysql.dumpStep: --single-transaction reads the InnoDB tables of each database at one point in time, without blocking writes.
mysql.compressStep: DBackup can compress each dump with Gzip or Brotli. The SQL inside stays plain text.
mysql.featureTitle: Three switches, and a check per database
mysql.featureText: Under Options, the source decides what goes into the dump. All three switches are on unless you turn them off.
mysql.featureNote: The password reaches the dump tool in a temporary file that only its owner can read, never on the command line.
mysql.archiveText: Pick some databases of a server, or leave the pick empty for all of them without the system schemas. Each gets its own dump in one TAR with a manifest and an index of checksums.
mysql.archive1: With an empty pick, the next run takes a new database along.
mysql.archive2: Restore one database under a new name, and the app rewrites its USE and CREATE DATABASE lines on the way in.
mysql.archive3: Unencrypted, the archive opens with tar -xf, and every dump is an SQL file, compressed with Gzip or Brotli when the job compresses.
mysql.restoreLead: Every dump is plain SQL made with --databases, so it creates and selects its own database. The Recovery Kit decrypts and unpacks it, and the mariadb client, the one DBackup restores with, reads it back.
mysql.userText: Read access for the dump, plus what the views, triggers and events need. LOCK TABLES only matters with the snapshot off.
mysql.q1: Which MySQL versions does DBackup support?
mysql.a1: MySQL 5.7 and newer. The integration tests run against 5.7 and 9.1. An older server gets a warning, and the dump still runs.
mysql.a2: In the Docker image it runs mariadb-dump, MariaDB's version of mysqldump, which dumps MySQL as well. Over SSH it takes mariadb-dump or mysqldump, whichever the server has.
mysql.q3: Are tables locked during the backup?
mysql.a3: Not with the consistent snapshot, which is on by default. It reads InnoDB tables at one point in time while writes carry on. Turn it off, and the tables of each database are locked while it is dumped.
mysql.q4: What does the backup user need?
mysql.a4: SELECT, SHOW VIEW, TRIGGER and EVENT, and LOCK TABLES when the snapshot is off. A restore that has to create a database asks for an admin login once.
mysql.q5: Can I restore a backup without DBackup?
mysql.a5: Yes. Every dump is a plain SQL file. The Recovery Kit gets it out, encrypted or not, and unpacks it, with nothing but Node.js. Then feed it to the mariadb client, the one DBackup restores with.

mariadb.description: Self-hosted MariaDB backups with mariadb-dump, the tool MariaDB ships itself. Consistent, with AES-256-GCM encryption and kept on S3, SFTP, a NAS or a cloud drive. Open source.
mariadb.lead: DBackup runs mariadb-dump, the tool MariaDB ships itself, on a schedule. It encrypts the dumps with AES-256-GCM when the job has a key, keeps them on the storage you choose and restores them with the mariadb client.
mariadb.fact2Label: MariaDB's client ships in the image
mariadb.fact3Label: Over SSH, mariadb-dump runs on your server
mariadb.fact4Label: Pick databases and give them new names
mariadb.dumpStep: mariadb-dump --single-transaction dumps each database from one consistent snapshot, with its routines and events by default.
mariadb.compressStep: DBackup can compress each dump with Gzip or Brotli before it is encrypted.
mariadb.featureTitle: What goes into the dump, per source
mariadb.featureText: The Options of a source decide. Each switch is on unless you turn it off, and Extra options go to mariadb-dump as they are.
mariadb.featureNote: The password reaches mariadb-dump in a temporary file that only its owner can read, never on the command line.
mariadb.archiveTitle: One archive per run, one dump per database
mariadb.archiveText: A job takes a single database, a few, or every database of the server without the system schemas. The dumps share one TAR with a manifest and an index of checksums.
mariadb.archive1: Restore a single database without touching the others, and give it a new name, like a copy next to the live one.
mariadb.archive2: A MariaDB backup restores into MariaDB only, and never from a newer server onto an older one. The app checks both before it starts.
mariadb.archive3: Unencrypted, tar -xf gets the SQL files out, and gunzip or brotli -d unpacks them when the job compresses.
mariadb.restoreLead: The Recovery Kit decrypts and unpacks a dump and checks it before it writes the file. The mariadb client does the rest.
mariadb.userText: Read access for the dump, plus what the views, triggers and events need. LOCK TABLES only matters with the snapshot off.
mariadb.q1: Which MariaDB versions does DBackup support?
mariadb.a1: MariaDB 10 and 11. The integration tests run against 10.11 and 11.4.
mariadb.q2: Can I restore a MariaDB backup into MySQL?
mariadb.a2: Not from the app, which refuses restores between MariaDB and MySQL and from a newer server onto an older one. The SQL file is still yours to import by hand.
mariadb.q3: Does a restore stop at the first error?
mariadb.a3: Yes. The mariadb client reads the dump without --force, so the first failing statement ends the restore, and the run shows the error.
mariadb.q4: Can DBackup back up a MariaDB server it cannot reach directly?
mariadb.a4: Yes, over SSH, which is in beta. DBackup logs into the server, runs mariadb-dump there and streams the dump back. The server needs mariadb-dump, mariadb and mariadb-admin, or their mysql names.
mariadb.q5: Can I restore a backup without DBackup?
mariadb.a5: Yes. The Recovery Kit gets the SQL file out, encrypted or not, and unpacks it, with nothing but Node.js. The mariadb client reads it back.

mongodb.description: Self-hosted MongoDB backups with mongodump, for MongoDB Atlas, replica sets and single servers. Encrypted with AES-256-GCM and kept on S3, SFTP, a NAS or a cloud drive. Open source.
mongodb.lead: DBackup runs mongodump on a schedule, against a single server, a replica set or MongoDB Atlas. It encrypts the archives with AES-256-GCM when the job has a key and restores them under any database name.
mongodb.fact3Label: Over SSH, mongodump runs on your server
mongodb.dumpStep: mongodump --archive --gzip writes one compressed archive per database, one after the other.
mongodb.compressStep: mongodump compresses the archive itself, so DBackup keeps it as it is and only encrypts it.
mongodb.featureTitle: Atlas, replica sets and single servers
mongodb.featureText: Type the host the way you know it. DBackup turns it into the right connection for mongodump.
mongodb.featureNote: The authentication database is admin unless you name another one.
mongodb.archiveText: Leave the pick empty and every run lists the databases again, without admin, config and local. Each one is dumped on its own into the same TAR.
mongodb.archive1: Restore a database under a new name, and mongorestore moves its collections with --nsFrom and --nsTo.
mongodb.archive2: A restore drops each collection before it writes it back, so the result matches the backup.
mongodb.archive3: Users and roles live in the admin database, which is not part of the backup.
mongodb.restoreLead: Each archive is what mongodump --gzip wrote. The Recovery Kit decrypts it, and mongorestore reads it back with the same flag.
mongodb.userText: The backup role reads every database, the restore role lets the app write it back.
mongodb.q1: Does DBackup work with MongoDB Atlas?
mongodb.a1: Yes. Enter the host of your cluster, like cluster0.abcde.mongodb.net, and DBackup connects through mongodb+srv on its own.
mongodb.q2: Is the backup a point-in-time snapshot?
mongodb.a2: No. mongodump runs without --oplog, so writes during the dump can be caught in part. For a busy database, schedule the job for a quiet hour.
mongodb.q3: Which MongoDB versions does DBackup support?
mongodb.a3: MongoDB 4 to 8. The image ships the MongoDB Database Tools 100.16, and the integration tests run against 4.4 and 8.0.
mongodb.q4: Are users and roles backed up?
mongodb.a4: No. They live in the admin database, which DBackup leaves out with config and local. Create the users on a new server before you restore.
mongodb.q5: Can I restore a backup without DBackup?
mongodb.a5: Yes. The Recovery Kit gets the archives out, encrypted or not, with nothing but Node.js. Then run mongorestore with --gzip and --archive.
mongodb.hostAtlas: An Atlas host is recognized and connected through mongodb+srv.
mongodb.hostSrv: Any other SRV record works once you write the scheme.
mongodb.hostSeeds: Several hosts become one connection to the replica set.
mongodb.hostSingle: A single server, with the port in its own field.

redis.description: Self-hosted Redis backups with redis-cli --rdb. Scheduled RDB snapshots, with AES-256-GCM encryption, kept on S3, SFTP, a NAS or a cloud drive, with a guided restore for Docker, Linux and Windows. Open source.
redis.heroTitle: Redis backups, <shine>with a restore that guides you.</shine>
redis.lead: DBackup takes an RDB snapshot with redis-cli --rdb on a schedule, encrypts it with AES-256-GCM when the job has a key and keeps it on the storage you choose. The restore page writes the script that puts it back.
redis.fact2Label: Every logical database in one file
redis.fact4Label: A script for Docker, Linux or Windows
redis.dumpStep: redis-cli --rdb asks the server for a snapshot, the same file a replica receives. It holds every logical database.
redis.compressStep: DBackup can compress the snapshot with Gzip or Brotli before it encrypts it.
redis.featureTitle: A restore that writes its own script
redis.featureText: Redis loads its snapshot when it starts, so a restore means stopping it and putting the file in place. The restore page writes a script for that, for the way your Redis runs.
redis.featureNote: Rather do it by hand? The Manual tab lists the same steps as commands.
redis.archiveText: An RDB file holds all logical databases of the server, so a backup is always one snapshot, whatever the job picked.
redis.archive1: A login is a Vault profile with a user and a password. For a server with only requirepass the user is default, from Redis 6 on. An ACL user needs SYNC, PSYNC, PING and INFO.
redis.archive2: Turn on TLS for a server that asks for it.
redis.archive3: Sentinel and Cluster are not supported yet. DBackup takes the snapshot of the one server you name.
redis.restoreLead: The snapshot is the RDB file Redis writes itself. The Recovery Kit decrypts and unpacks it, and Redis loads it on the next start.
redis.userTitle: Or give DBackup a user of its own
redis.userText: With Redis 6 and newer, an ACL user with these four commands is enough for the backup and the health check.
redis.q1: Does the snapshot hold every database?
redis.a1: Yes. An RDB file holds all logical databases of the server, and DBackup stores it as one entry.
redis.q2: What if Redis writes an append-only file?
redis.a2: With appendonly on, Redis loads the AOF at start and ignores the RDB. The restore guide has a part for that case, and its script stops before it changes anything while appendonly is on.
redis.q3: Does DBackup support Redis Cluster or Sentinel?
redis.a3: Not yet. DBackup connects to the one server you name and takes its snapshot.
redis.q4: Which Redis versions does DBackup support?
redis.a4: Redis 2.8 and newer, and Valkey 7.2 and newer through its own source type. The integration tests run against Redis 6 and 8.
redis.q5: Can I restore a backup without DBackup?
redis.a5: Yes. The Recovery Kit gets dump.rdb out, encrypted or not, and unpacks it, with nothing but Node.js. Stop Redis, put the file in its data folder and start it again.
redis.guide1: Checks PING, appendonly, dir and dbfilename before it changes anything
redis.guide2: Stops Redis and keeps the old snapshot as dump.rdb.before-restore
redis.guide3: Puts the backup in place and starts Redis again
redis.guide4: Waits until Redis answers and shows INFO keyspace
redis.guideScript: A bash script, or PowerShell for Windows, to download or copy.
